title: India's Cash Paradox: Currency in Circulation Surges Past ₹41 Lakh Crore Despite UPI Boom
excerpt: SBI Research finds cash holdings have hit their highest growth rate since post-demonetisation 2016, even as UPI processes over ₹314 trillion annually — driven by GST enforcement fears, rural consumption, and a rising precautionary motive.
body:
• Currency in circulation surged 11.9% in FY26 to an all-time high of ₹41.6 lakh crore — the highest growth since post-demonetisation 2016
  • UPI transactions simultaneously hit ₹314 trillion in FY26, with volumes jumping 30% to 241.6 billion
  • The cash-to-GDP ratio has declined to 11% from 14.4% in FY21, showing the economy is growing faster than cash demand
  • GST notices to 18,000 small traders in Karnataka for UPI transactions above ₹40 lakh spooked vendors across multiple states into preferring cash

India's currency in circulation reached an all-time high of ₹41.6 lakh crore by the end of FY26, growing at 11.9% year-on-year — the fastest pace since the post-demonetisation remonetisation of 2016, according to SBI Research. The surge continued through early 2026, with currency with public (CWP) crossing ₹39 lakh crore by January alone, accounting for 97.6% of all circulated currency.

The numbers present a puzzle. At the same time, India's Unified Payments Interface processed ₹314 trillion worth of transactions in FY26, with volumes jumping 30% to 241.6 billion. Monthly UPI transaction value stood at roughly ₹28 lakh crore — about 70% of the entire currency stock. Both cash and digital payments are expanding simultaneously.

What's Driving the Cash Surge

SBI Research identified several converging factors. The most immediate was a compliance scare: Karnataka's Commercial Taxes Department issued approximately 18,000 GST notices to small traders and vendors whose UPI transactions exceeded the ₹40 lakh registration threshold between 2022 and 2025. The enforcement action had a chilling effect well beyond Karnataka, with ATM withdrawal patterns spiking in states including West Bengal and Kerala as vendors shifted back to cash to avoid digital paper trails.

"Despite an increase in CiC, cash as a percentage of GDP is declining, and ATM cash withdrawal as a percentage of GDP is also declining. This clearly indicates that digital transactions continue to dominate our economy."

— Soumya Kanti Ghosh, Group Chief Economic Adviser, SBI

Broader macroeconomic forces also played a role. Lower interest rates encouraged consumption, particularly in rural areas, where the propensity to hold cash remains high. The withdrawal of ₹2,000 denomination notes forced a denomination shift into ₹100, ₹200, and ₹500 notes, increasing the total number of notes in circulation. Rising precious metal prices may have led to liquidation into cash.

The Precautionary Motive

A striking finding from SBI Research is the widening gap between per capita currency held and ATM withdrawals. This gap jumped from ₹1,804 in FY24 to ₹9,127 in FY26 — a five-fold increase in just two years. Researchers attributed this to a rising precautionary motive, amplified by social media-driven uncertainty. People are hoarding cash rather than spending or depositing it.

Small-ticket transactions tell a different story: 86% of person-to-merchant UPI transactions are below ₹500, and roughly 60% of person-to-person transfers fall under the same threshold. For everyday spending, digital rails have clearly won. Cash serves a different function — as a store of liquidity, a hedge against uncertainty, and a medium for informal transactions that resist formalisation.

Less-Cash, Not Cashless

The data points to what analysts describe as a hybrid equilibrium. India's cash-to-GDP ratio has declined steadily to 11% in FY26 from 14.4% during the pandemic year of FY21, confirming that the economy's incremental growth is increasingly financed by UPI rather than currency. But in absolute terms, a larger economy simply carries more cash.

SBI Research cautioned policymakers against disincentivising digital platforms, arguing that India's structural transition toward digital payments remains intact despite the elevated absolute cash levels. The destination, as one analysis put it, is a less-cash economy — not a cashless one.
